title: Fewest Terms to Finish Every Course
statement:
A program has n courses labelled 1 to n. Each pair [before, after] in prereqs means course before must be finished in an earlier term than course after is taken.

In one term a student can take any number of courses, as long as all their prerequisites were finished in earlier terms. Return the fewest terms needed to finish all n courses, or -1 if the prerequisites make that impossible.

examples.why: Courses 1 and 2 go together in term 1, course 3 in term 2.
The chain 1 → 2 → 3 sets the length. Course 4 and 5 fit in alongside it. The answer is the longest chain, not the number of prerequisites.
The three courses wait on each other in a loop, so none of them can ever start.

hints: Which courses can go in term 1? Exactly the ones with no prerequisites.
Take all of them in term 1, cross them off, and ask the same question again. Doing this efficiently is a topological sort, level by level.
Kahn's algorithm with a queue: count incoming edges, start with every zero-count course, and process one whole level per term. If some course is never processed, there is a cycle.

explain.intuition:
Taking a course as early as possible never hurts, because there is no limit per term. So the greedy plan is: every term, take everything that is unlocked. Term 1 holds all courses with no prerequisites; term 2 holds those whose prerequisites were all in term 1; and so on. The number of terms equals the longest prerequisite chain.

That is breadth-first topological sorting. Keep for each course how many unfinished prerequisites it has (its in-degree). The courses at zero form the first level. Finishing a level lowers the counts of the courses that depend on it, and those that drop to zero form the next level. If the levels run out before every course is taken, the remaining courses wait on each other in a loop, and the answer is -1. Build tools that run independent tasks in parallel use the same plan.
steps: Build an adjacency list next[before] and an in-degree count for every course.
Put every course with in-degree 0 into the current level.
While the level is not empty: count a term, and for each course in it decrease the in-degree of each course in next; those reaching 0 go into the next level.
Count how many courses were taken in total. If it is less than n, return -1; otherwise return the number of terms.
pitfalls: Returning the number of prerequisite pairs or the number of courses. The answer is the longest chain, as the second example shows.
Mixing levels in a single queue without tracking where one term ends, which counts courses instead of terms.
Forgetting the cycle check. A cycle that does not touch the starting courses, as in [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2]], still makes it impossible.

solutions.title: Repeated sweeps
solutions.idea: Each term, scan all prerequisite pairs to find courses whose prerequisites are all finished, and take them together. Stop when a sweep takes nothing.

solutions.title: Topological sort level by level
solutions.idea: Kahn's algorithm. Every level of zero in-degree courses is one term.

followups: Now a student may take at most k courses per term. Why does the greedy level approach stop being optimal?
Each course also has a length in weeks and courses run in parallel. How long until everything is done?
